balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

cet1.title: CET1 ratio
cet1.content:
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is core regulatory capital (ordinary equity less deductions) divided by risk-weighted assets. It is the standard measure of a bank's loss-absorbing capacity and the regulator's binding constraint on dividends and buybacks.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the Board targets c.13.0%; the DCF's 'capex' line is exactly the CET1 retention needed to hold that ratio as RWAs grow, so this chart is the input the valuation's reinvestment rate is built from.

What to watch:

  • Ratio falling toward or through the c.13% target (pressures buybacks)
  • One-off RWA inflation (e.g. motor-finance provision, model changes)
  • Pro forma ratio after announced buybacks and dividends, disclosed alongside the reported figure

niiOpex.title: Net interest income vs operating expenses
niiOpex.content:
Net interest income (NII) is interest earned on loans and the structural hedge less interest paid on deposits and wholesale funding -- the core revenue engine of a retail/commercial bank. Operating expenses is the cost base run against it; their ratio is the bank's cost:income ratio.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: FY26 guidance targets cost:income below 50%; NII benefits from the structural hedge rolling onto higher rates even as deposit margins compress.

What to watch:

  • Opex growing faster than NII (cost:income drifting up)
  • NII trend versus the policy rate cycle, not just the headline number
  • One-off items in opex (e.g. the FY2025 motor-finance charge) that distort the trend

deposits.title: Customer deposits
deposits.content:
Customer deposits are the bank's primary and cheapest source of funding. For a bank, deposits are operating liabilities, not debt -- they fund the loan book rather than encumber the balance sheet, which is why the DCF does not deduct them as net debt.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: a c.GBP 500bn deposit base funds the mortgage-heavy loan book and anchors the structural hedge that drives NII.

What to watch:

  • Deposit growth or outflow relative to loan growth (funding gap)
  • Mix shift from current accounts into higher-cost savings (margin pressure)

impairment.title: Credit impairment charge
impairment.content:
Credit impairment charge is the expected-credit-loss provision booked against the loan book each period -- the accounting cost of credit risk. A negative value is a release (prior provisions written back).

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: FY26 guidance is an asset quality ratio (AQR) of c.25bps; FY2020's GBP 4.2bn charge and FY2021's GBP 1.4bn release bracket the COVID cycle and show how volatile this line can be relative to the through-cycle run-rate the base case assumes.

What to watch:

  • Charge rising well above the c.25-30bps through-cycle guide (credit quality deteriorating)
  • Large one-off releases that flatter a single year's profit

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
